title: The Song of Deborah
summary: Deborah and Barak sing a victory hymn celebrating the LORD's triumph over Sisera. The song pictures God marching from Seir with storm and earthquake, remembers how life in Israel's villages had collapsed, praises the tribes who volunteered and rebukes those who stayed home, and describes the stars and the Kishon fighting against Sisera. It lingers over Jael's killing of Sisera and ends with his mother waiting at her window for a son who will never return.
story: Chapter 4 told the victory over Jabin and Sisera in prose. Chapter 5 retells it as poetry, in the manner of the Song of the Sea after the exodus (Exodus 15), where prose narrative is followed by a hymn. The song adds details the prose leaves out: the storm, the flood of the Kishon, the tribes who came and those who didn't, and the scene of Sisera's mother. It is Israel's worshiping response to what God has done, and it shows how the people remembered and sang their history. It ends with the formula of the book: the land had rest for forty years.
historical:
Many scholars regard the Song of Deborah as one of the oldest substantial pieces of Hebrew literature, perhaps composed not long after the events it describes, around the twelfth century BC on the common dating. Its Hebrew is archaic and difficult in places, with rare words and old grammatical forms, which is why translations differ widely on some verses (especially 10 to 15). Others argue that archaic style can be deliberately imitated and prefer a later date, but the song's early origin is widely held.

The song gives a picture of Israel before the monarchy. The tribes are a loose alliance, and participation in war is voluntary. Ten are mentioned: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir (a clan of Manasseh), Zebulun, Issachar, and Naphtali joined the fight; Reuben, Gilead (the tribes east of the Jordan), Dan, and Asher did not. Judah and Simeon aren't mentioned at all, perhaps because they were too far south or not yet closely bound to the northern tribes. The battle site is placed at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo, in the Jezreel Valley. Meroz, the town cursed for not coming (verse 23), is otherwise unknown.
cultural:
Victory songs sung by women were part of Israel's culture, as when Miriam led the women with tambourines after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:20-21) and when the women sang of Saul and David (1 Samuel 18:6-7). Singers at the watering places (verse 11), where people gathered to draw water, retold the LORD's righteous acts, which shows how stories were passed on in an oral culture.

The opening image of the LORD marching from Seir and Edom, with the earth trembling and the sky pouring rain, draws on the tradition that God came from the south, from the region of Sinai, to help his people. Similar language appears in Deuteronomy 33:2, Psalm 68:7-8, and Habakkuk 3:3. The storm imagery also sets the LORD against Baal, the Canaanite storm god: it is Israel's God who commands the rain and the flood. The final scene reflects the grim reality of ancient warfare, in which victorious soldiers took captive women and plunder, including fine dyed and embroidered cloth, a valuable luxury.
literary: The song is Hebrew poetry, built on parallel lines in which the second line repeats, extends, or sharpens the first, and it uses a staircase technique typical of very old Canaanite and Hebrew verse, where a phrase is repeated and then built upon, as in verse 27: "At her feet he collapsed, he fell, there he lay still." The song moves in sections: a call to praise (2 and 3), the LORD's coming in storm (4 and 5), Israel's distress before Deborah (6 to 8), a call to remember (9 to 11), the roll call of tribes (12 to 18), the battle (19 to 22), the curse on Meroz and blessing on Jael (23 to 27), and the scene of Sisera's mother (28 to 30), before a closing prayer (31). The last scene is a masterpiece of irony: the reader knows Sisera is dead, while his mother and her ladies imagine him dividing the spoil. The prose account's woman with the tent peg is matched by another woman at a window, waiting.

outline.t: A call to bless the LORD
The LORD marches from Seir in storm
The tribes who came and those who stayed away
The battle: stars and river fight for Israel
Meroz cursed, Jael blessed, Sisera falls
Sisera's mother waits at the window
Closing prayer and forty years of rest

doctrines.note: The LORD is pictured as a divine warrior who comes in storm and earthquake to fight for his people, commanding even the stars and the river. The victory belongs to him.
The song is an act of worship: Israel responds to deliverance by blessing the LORD and telling his righteous acts. Praise that remembers is one of Scripture's basic forms of prayer.

The roll call of the tribes shows that belonging to God's people carries a call to stand with one another. Some tribes risked their lives; others stayed by their sheepfolds and harbors, and the song names both.

words.note: Nadav, to offer freely or volunteer. The song opens and returns to the people who volunteered (verses 2 and 9). The same root describes freewill offerings. The victory depended on people who gave themselves willingly.

Tsedaqah, righteousness. In verse 11 the plural means righteous acts, the saving deeds by which the LORD put things right for his oppressed people. Righteousness here is not only a quality but action: God setting wrong right.

Em, mother. Deborah calls herself a mother in Israel (verse 7), a title of honor and care for the people. The song closes with another mother, Sisera's, waiting in vain. The two mothers frame the victory from opposite sides.

Racham, womb. In verse 30 the phrase translated a girl or two is literally a womb, two wombs, a crude soldier's expression for captive women. The ugly word shows what Sisera's victories meant for Israel's daughters, and why his defeat was deliverance.

christ: The song celebrates the LORD as a warrior who comes to save his people when they cannot save themselves. The New Testament presents Christ's victory as the defeat of the powers of evil, though won by his own suffering rather than by the sword (Colossians 2:15). The closing prayer, that those who love the LORD would shine like the sun, finds an echo in Jesus' words that the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom (Matthew 13:43). The connection here is thematic. The song's longing for God's enemies to perish and his friends to shine is answered in the New Testament in a way that includes the offer of reconciliation to enemies.

hard.q: How can a song in Scripture gloat over a man's death and mock his grieving mother?
hard.a: The ending is unsettling. Some readers hear cruelty in it. Others read the scene of Sisera's mother as more complex than gloating: it exposes the reality behind Sisera's glory, since his mother imagines captured Israelite women and plunder, the very things Israel had suffered under him for twenty years. The irony turns the violence of the oppressor back on him. Some interpreters also hear a note of pathos, even sympathy, in the portrait of a mother waiting at the window. The song was written from the side of an oppressed people rejoicing in their deliverance, and Scripture includes such songs honestly. Later Scripture, especially Jesus' command to love enemies, sets a further light on how God's people should regard even those who oppress them.

questions: The song praises those who volunteered and rebukes those who stayed home. Where is God calling you to stand with others rather than stay by your sheepfolds?
Verse 11 describes people retelling God's acts at the wells. How do you pass on the stories of what God has done?
What do you make of the scene of Sisera's mother? Does it change how you feel about the victory?
